text: Chapter 1 got Terraform installed and a provider configured on your machine. Before Northbridge Retail's platform team writes a single real resource, you need to be fluent in the language every Terraform file is written in: HashiCorp Configuration Language, or HCL.

Every HCL file is built from blocks. A block has a type, optional quoted labels, and a body in curly braces. Here, "locals" is the block type, it takes no labels, and each line inside the body is an argument: a name, an equals sign, and a value. You'll meet blocks with one or two labels starting next lesson.

Arguments can hold five kinds of values. Strings are quoted text, numbers and booleans have no quotes at all. A list is an ordered, square-bracketed sequence, like a set of allowed regions. A map is an unordered set of key-value pairs in curly braces, like a block of tags. You'll use every one of these constantly once you start writing real resource and variable blocks.

HCL supports two comment styles. The hash symbol is what you'll see in almost every official example and throughout this course. Two slashes work identically, borrowed from other languages. A slash-star block comment can span multiple lines, which is handy for temporarily disabling a whole block while you're testing something else.

When you need a value dropped into the middle of a string, HCL uses dollar-sign curly-brace interpolation. Anything inside gets evaluated as an expression — a variable reference, even a function call — and the result is spliced into the surrounding string. You'll lean on this constantly once resource names need to incorporate an environment or project name.
That's the full grammar you need to read and write any Terraform file. Next up, Lesson 7: resource and provider blocks, the two block types that actually create infrastructure.
